papers.title: When History Helps and Hurts: Selective History Use across Multimodal Turns
papers.abstract: Reliable multimodal interaction depends on selective use of conversational history: an earlier question may remain relevant while its previous answer is outdated, whereas a current request may depend on historical evidence despite conflicting new observations. Existing multi-turn evaluations rarely separate these history-use demands from underlying question difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce ReTurn, a benchmark of 7,000 base tasks spanning visual and audio evidence for evaluating selective history use. For task-carrying history, Reconfirm/Reground require applying a historical question to current media while varying historical agreement; for evidence-carrying history, Retrieve/Rebind require answering a current question using historical media while varying current-media competition. Each pair preserves the target question, media, and answer. Tasks support open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation, with matched single-turn counterparts serving as answerability references. Across 13 omni-modal, vision-language, and audio-language models, median model-level open-ended accuracy falls from 93.7% with direct input to 72.3% in conversation. Behavioral probes show that high question recall can coexist with weaker task application, while competing media can redirect answers away from historical targets. Supervised adaptation yields only partial gains. ReTurn provides a controlled framework for assessing whether multimodal models select and use the historical information required by each request.

papers.title: Listen-to-Reason: Listen with Experts, Retrieve over a Graph, Reason with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) fuse an audio encoder into a large language model (LLM) through multi-stage training. This coupling means that a new domain or a stronger LLM requires retraining, and their answers cannot be traced to what the model heard: a chain-of-thought is a post-hoc account. We propose Listen-to-Reason (L2R), an interpretable-by-design pipeline that passes audio to the LLM through an explicit, human-readable tree: small heads on frozen expert encoders map each chunk of a clip to semantically meaningful nodes on the tree (for speech, music and environmental sound), and a frozen text-only LLM answers from these nodes and an ASR transcript without hearing the clip. Every answer can therefore be traced to the nodes and transcript it read, and the nodes are causal: replacing the deciding node with a distractor overturns 78% of correct answers on SAKURA. With a 7B reader, L2R outperforms all LALMs we compare against on SAKURA and trails them by 6-12 points on MMAU and MMAR, despite training about 1,400x fewer parameters on orders of magnitude less audio data. However, because any LLM can serve as the reader, we show that a stronger reader narrows this gap without retraining any audio component. A new domain is added with one small head: with five labelled clips per species, it outperforms QLoRA fine-tuning of an LALM on the same clips by 13-26 points.

papers.title: Conversational Voice Aesthetic Model with Reinforcement Learning from Human Listeners
papers.abstract: We introduce Conversational Voice Aesthetic Model, a speech large language model for describing the voice aesthetics of real or synthetic speech responses in natural conversational contexts. Given a context and a response speech, CVAM describes salient moments that characterize the voice and predicts nine categorical attributes spanning gender, pitch, pacing, emotion, and delivery. The key challenge lies in perceptual fields such as emotion and delivery, which are inherently subjective and lack definitive ground truth. Therefore, we collect ~10 human annotations for each of 3k real and synthetic responses derived from the CANDOR corpus. CVAM is supervised finetuned on synthesized aesthetic descriptions and labels, then optimized with Group Relative Policy Optimization on human judgments. Experiments show that CVAM better agrees with human listeners than Gemini 3.1 Pro and open-source speech LLMs, and outperforms single-human-vs.-rest agreement. Together, we demonstrate the importance of grounding voice aesthetics in human perception and propose a principled framework for human alignment.

papers.title: Edukasi Literasi Digital sebagai Respons terhadap Krisis Disinformasi Berbasis AI pada Komunitas Perempuan di Bintara, Kota Bekasi
papers.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence—such as deepfakes and voice cloning—is accelerating the spread of disinformation in Indonesia and eroding public trust in digital information. Mothers serve as key nodes for information distribution within family ecosystems but are prone to sharing information without verification. The "Cek Sebelum Cekcok" (Check Before Conflict) community service program was designed to strengthen the digital literacy of women aged 30–50 in Bintara Urban Village, Bekasi City—specifically targeting elderly members of the Prolanis program identified through social mapping—grounded in the frameworks of cyberethics (Ess, 2009) and post-truth epistemology (McIntyre, 2018). Program implementation began with participatory social mapping involving field observations and informal interviews, followed by an in-person talk show featuring speakers from academia, regulatory bodies, and the digital industry, alongside participant comprehension assessments using pre-test and post-test instruments. Social mapping revealed that the ecosystem of resident conversation networks is not homogeneous: Neighborhood Association (RT) groups were relatively safe from hoaxes, whereas Community Association (RW) groups and Prolanis groups were most vulnerable to manipulative content; consequently, digital literacy interventions needed to be tailored to each network layer rather than employing a uniform approach. Pre- and post-test results from 150 respondents showed an improvement in the ability to identify AI-generated content: the proportion of respondents who correctly identified all videos rose from 11.3% (17 respondents) in the pre-test to 68.0% (102 respondents) in the post-test. The program recommends replicating this intervention model—based on social mapping and network differentiation—in other urban areas with similar characteristics, alongside continuous monitoring of changes in information verification behavior.

# Music-LLM 45M — a compact text-to-music transformer

A 44.9M-parameter MusicGen-style autoregressive transformer that generates
music audio from short text prompts, implemented **in pure PyTorch** — the
attention layers, training loop, generation sampler, and the two-GPU pipeline
parallelism it was trained with are all hand-written, without training
frameworks.

This model was built **for research and education** — to demonstrate, end to
end, how a text-to-music LLM is constructed and trained. It is a **small
model** (45M parameters, 8 hours of training audio, 10 genre captions), so
please do not expect the high-quality music of large production models: it
generates genre-flavoured musical texture rather than finished songs. Its
value is the fully readable, fully explainable implementation and training
story.

> **Newer version:** [**music-llm-45m-fma**](https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m-fma)
> is this same architecture, continued from these weights and trained on the
> Free Music Archive (about 25× more clips, 15 genres).

## 🔊 Samples

Generated by this exact checkpoint (30 s each, CFG 3.0, top-k 250). Press play:

**"jazz music"**
<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m/resolve/main/samples/music-jazz-pp.wav"></audio>

**"metal music"**
<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m/resolve/main/samples/music-metal-pp.wav"></audio>

**"classical music"**
<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m/resolve/main/samples/music-classical-pp.wav"></audio>

[Download: jazz](samples/music-jazz-pp.wav) · [metal](samples/music-metal-pp.wav) · [classical](samples/music-classical-pp.wav)

## Architecture

![Architecture: text prompt through frozen T5 into an 8-block transformer decoder with cross-attention, four 2048-way heads, decoded to audio by frozen EnCodec](architecture.png)

| component | detail |
|---|---|
| audio tokens | EnCodec 32 kHz: 4 codebooks × 2048 tokens @ 50 Hz, delay pattern |
| decoder | 8 blocks, d=512, 8 heads, pre-LayerNorm, GELU |
| conditioning | frozen T5-base (768-d) via cross-attention in every block |
| guidance | classifier-free guidance (caption dropout 0.2 at train time) |
| heads | 4 parallel 2048-way softmax heads, masked cross-entropy |
| parameters | 44,876,800 (EnCodec and T5 excluded — frozen, loaded at runtime) |

## 🚀 How to use

**Can `transformers.AutoModel` load this? No** — it is a custom architecture,
not a `transformers` model. Instead, everything needed to run it lives in a
single file: `example.py` contains the full model definition and the
generation loop, so three commands get you generating:

```bash
pip install torch numpy transformers sentencepiece soundfile huggingface_hub
hf download khashayargh/music-llm-45m --local-dir music-llm-45m
cd music-llm-45m && python example.py "jazz music" --seconds 15
```

(`transformers` is used only to load the frozen T5 and EnCodec components,
which download automatically on first run.)

Trained prompts: `"<genre> music"` for blues, classical, country, disco,
hiphop, jazz, metal, pop, reggae, rock. Runs on CUDA, Apple Silicon (MPS),
or CPU; 15 s of audio takes a few minutes on a laptop.

## Training

![Training and validation loss of the production run](training-curves.png)

- **Data**: GTZAN (999 clips, 10 genres, ~8 h), random 20-second windows
- **Hardware**: 2× NVIDIA RTX A6000 via **hand-written GPipe-style pipeline
  parallelism** (stage 1: embedding + blocks 1–4; stage 2: blocks 5–8 + heads),
  4 micro-batches, valid-token-weighted gradient accumulation with
  test-proven exact parity to single-device training
- **Recipe**: AdamW, peak lr ≈ 5e-4 (Optuna TPE search run through the real
  pipeline under the production lr schedule), 1000-step warmup + cosine decay,
  gradient clipping, non-finite-step guard
- **This checkpoint**: step 4,000 — the validation-loss minimum (val ≈ 5.98),
  saved automatically before the train/val curves diverged (early stopping
  against overfitting on the small corpus)
- War story: the first runs produced infinite gradients that were root-caused
  to **silent PCIe peer-to-peer corruption** on the host machine; the pipeline
  detects this at startup and reroutes its stage boundary through CPU memory
  at ~0.3% overhead. Hardware-level debugging is part of distributed training.

## Limitations

- **Small model, small data — by design.** Education-scale: expect texture
  and genre flavour, not melody, structure, or production quality
- Trained on **10 captions total** ("blues music" … "rock music") — it cannot
  follow free-form descriptions; prompt steering is coarse
- GTZAN-derived: **research / educational use only** (hence CC-BY-NC-4.0)
- Mono, 32 kHz

## Project

Built by [Khashayar Ghamati](https://ghamati.com).
The full story — architecture, the two-GPU pipeline, the PCIe bug hunt, real
training curves, and audio to judge:
**[Building a Small Transformer That Makes Music](https://ghamati.com/blog/music-llm/)**

# Music-LLM 45M (FMA) — the same compact text-to-music transformer, trained on far more music

This is the second release of [Music-LLM 45M](https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m):
the **same 44.9M-parameter architecture**, continued from that model's weights
and trained on the **Free Music Archive (FMA medium)** — about 25 times more
clips and 15 genres instead of 10. Everything is implemented in pure PyTorch,
including the two-GPU pipeline parallelism it was trained with.

It is built **for research and education**, to show end to end how a
text-to-music LLM is constructed and trained. It is a **small model**: please
do not expect the quality of large production systems. It produces
genre-flavoured musical texture, not finished songs.

|  | [music-llm-45m](https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m) | **this model** |
|---|---|---|
| training data | GTZAN: 999 clips, ~8 h | FMA medium: 24,742 clips, ~206 h |
| genre prompts | 10 | 15 |
| start | random weights | weights of music-llm-45m (step 4,000) |
| training | 4,000 steps (best checkpoint) | 20,000 steps |
| validation loss | 5.998 (GTZAN clips) | **5.410** (FMA clips) |
| parameters | 44,876,800 | 44,876,800 |

**The two validation losses are not comparable**: they are measured on
different held-out music. A lower loss means the model predicts FMA audio
tokens better; it does not by itself mean it sounds better, and I make no such
claim. Judge by ear below.

## Architecture

| component | detail |
|---|---|
| audio tokens | EnCodec 32 kHz: 4 codebooks × 2048 tokens @ 50 Hz, delay pattern |
| decoder | 8 blocks, d=512, 8 heads, pre-LayerNorm, GELU |
| conditioning | frozen T5-base (768-d) via cross-attention in every block |
| guidance | classifier-free guidance (caption dropout 0.2 at train time) |

| parameters | 44,876,800 (EnCodec and T5 excluded — frozen, loaded at runtime) |

## 🚀 How to use

**Can `transformers.AutoModel` load this? No** — it is a custom architecture,
not a `transformers` model. Everything needed lives in one file: `example.py`
contains the full model definition and the generation loop.

```bash
pip install torch numpy transformers sentencepiece soundfile huggingface_hub
hf download khashayargh/music-llm-45m-fma --local-dir music-llm-45m-fma
cd music-llm-45m-fma && python example.py "jazz music" --seconds 15
```

(`transformers` is used only to load the frozen T5 and EnCodec components,
which download automatically on first run.)

**Prompt exactly as trained**: `"<genre> music"` in lowercase, for one of
blues, classical, country, easy listening, electronic, experimental, folk,
hip-hop, instrumental, international, jazz, old-time / historic, pop, rock,
soul-rnb. Other wording (for example a bare label like `"Blues"`) is outside
what it was trained on. Runs on CUDA, Apple Silicon (MPS) or CPU.

## Training

![Training curves: loss, per-step loss, learning rate and gradient norm over 20,000 steps](training-curves.png)

- **Data**: FMA medium (Defferrard et al., 2017): 24,882 30-second clips in 15
  top-level genres (the "Spoken" genre is excluded, it is speech, not music).
  After dropping unreadable and too-short files, 24,742 clips are used for
  training and 120 are held out for validation (8 per genre); training draws
  random 20-second windows.
- **Start**: weights of `music-llm-45m`; the optimizer, learning-rate schedule
  and step counter start fresh.
- **Recipe**: AdamW, peak lr 5.23e-4 (found by an Optuna search on the GTZAN
  model and **not re-tuned** for FMA), 1,000-step warmup then cosine decay to
  5.2e-5, batch 16 × 20 s, gradient clipping at 1.0, float32.
- **Hardware**: 2× NVIDIA RTX A6000 with hand-written GPipe-style pipeline
  parallelism (blocks 1–4 on one GPU, 5–8 plus heads on the other). The
  20,000 steps took about 25 hours. The model is so small that each GPU peaked
  at only ~2.5 GB, so the hardware was mostly idle on memory.
- **This checkpoint**: step 20,000, which was also the validation minimum
  (val 5.410). The loss was still creeping down by about 0.001 per 200 steps
  at the end, so more training would help only a little.

## Limitations

- **Small model, by design.** Education-scale: expect texture and genre
  flavour, not melody, structure or production quality.
- **Coarse prompts.** It saw 15 two-word captions, so it cannot follow free-form
  descriptions.
- **Noisy labels.** FMA genre tags are assigned by uploaders and are loose, so
  "pop" or "international" cover very different sounds.
- **Licence.** FMA tracks carry various Creative Commons licences, many of them
  non-commercial, so this model is for **research and educational use only**
  (CC-BY-NC-4.0).
- Mono, 32 kHz.

# Music-LLM 1B (FMA) — the same text-to-music recipe, 23× more parameters

This is the large sibling of [Music-LLM 45M (FMA)](https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m-fma):
**1,027,018,752 parameters** (d = 2048, 16 blocks, 16 heads) trained on the same
**Free Music Archive (FMA medium)** data, with the same four-codebook EnCodec token
format and the same frozen T5 prompt encoder. Everything is implemented in pure
PyTorch, including the two-GPU pipeline parallelism it was trained with.

It is built **for research and education**, to show what changes, and what does
not, when only the model size changes. It is still a **small model by music-AI
standards**: do not expect the quality of large production systems. It produces
genre-flavoured musical texture, not finished songs.

|  | [music-llm-45m-fma](https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m-fma) | **this model** |
|---|---|---|
| parameters | 44,876,800 | **1,027,018,752** |
| decoder | 8 blocks, d = 512, 8 heads | **16 blocks, d = 2048, 16 heads** |
| training data | FMA medium, 15 genres | FMA medium, 15 genres (same) |
| start | weights of the GTZAN model | **random weights** |
| training | 20,000 steps, batch 16 | **12,000 steps, batch 32** |
| precision | float32 | **bfloat16 compute, float32 weights** |
| learning rate (peak) | 5.23e-4 | **9.51e-5** (searched, see below) |
| dropout | 0.014 | 0.1 |
| wall-clock | about 25 h | **10.3 h** (2× RTX A6000) |

## What the larger model buys (measured)

The two training runs report validation loss on **different held-out sets** and
with different evaluation code, so their logged numbers (5.362 for this model,
5.410 for the 45M) must not be compared. To compare fairly, both checkpoints were
scored on the **same 120 FMA clips that neither model trained on** (8 per genre,
first and last 20-second window of each clip, 960,000 predicted tokens each):

| on the same 120 held-out clips | 45M | **1B** |
|---|---|---|
| cross-entropy (nats per audio token) | 5.355 | **5.320** |
| model's own entropy | 5.378 | 5.161 |

So 23× more parameters bought **0.035 nats** — a real but small gain. The
models also disagree with each other much more than that gap suggests:
KL(1B ‖ 45M) = 0.229 nats per token and Jensen-Shannon divergence = 0.054
(its maximum is 0.693), so they are different predictors of similar accuracy,
not one model plus noise.

![Per-codebook gain and disagreement, sharpness, and per-genre gain](kl-results.png)

- **Coarse codebook gains most.** The cross-entropy gap is 0.043 on the first (coarsest)
  codebook and 0.025 on the last.
- **Genres differ a lot.** Gain per genre ranges from +0.104 (electronic) and +0.055
  (hip-hop) down to +0.013 (rock), +0.012 (jazz) and +0.006 (instrumental). Across
  the 15 genres, the gain correlates with how much the two models disagree (r = 0.81).
- **The 1B is sharper than it is right.** On held-out clips its own entropy (5.16)
  is lower than its actual cross-entropy (5.32): it is somewhat over-confident, a sign
  of a model that has started to fit its training clips (see training section).
  The 45M is the opposite (5.38 vs 5.36).

Measured on 120 clips per model pair, a single run each: treat the per-genre numbers
as indicative, not precise.

## 🔊 Samples

A lower loss means the model predicts FMA audio tokens better; it does not by
itself mean it sounds better, and no such claim is made. Judge by ear.

## Architecture

![Architecture: text prompt through frozen T5 into a 16-block transformer decoder with cross-attention, four 2048-way heads, decoded to audio by frozen EnCodec](architecture.png)

| component | detail |
|---|---|
| audio tokens | EnCodec 32 kHz: 4 codebooks × 2048 tokens @ 50 Hz, delay pattern |
| decoder | 16 blocks, d = 2048, 16 heads, MLP 2048 → 8192 → 2048, pre-LayerNorm, GELU |
| conditioning | frozen T5-base (768-d) via cross-attention in every block |
| guidance | classifier-free guidance (caption dropout 0.2 at train time) |
| heads | 4 parallel 2048-way softmax heads, masked cross-entropy |
| context | 1,500 frames = 30 s |
| parameters | 1,027,018,752 (EnCodec and T5 excluded — frozen, loaded at runtime) |

## 🚀 How to use

**Can `transformers.AutoModel` load this? No** — it is a custom architecture,
not a `transformers` model. Everything needed lives in one file: `example.py`
contains the full model definition and the generation loop, and reads the model
size from the checkpoint.

```bash
pip install torch numpy transformers sentencepiece soundfile huggingface_hub
hf download khashayargh/music-llm-1b-fma --local-dir music-llm-1b-fma
cd music-llm-1b-fma && python example.py "jazz music" --seconds 15
```

The weights file is 4.3 GB (float32). Generation needs roughly 6 GB of free GPU or
unified memory for the model; it runs on CUDA, Apple Silicon (MPS) or CPU (slowly).
`transformers` is used only to load the frozen T5 and EnCodec components, which
download automatically on first run.

**Prompt exactly as trained**: `"<genre> music"` in lowercase, for one of
blues, classical, country, easy listening, electronic, experimental, folk,
hip-hop, instrumental, international, jazz, old-time / historic, pop, rock,
soul-rnb. Other wording (for example a bare label like `"Blues"`) is outside
what it was trained on.

## Training

![Training curves: loss, per-step loss, learning rate and gradient norm over 12,000 steps](training-curves.png)

- **Data**: FMA medium (Defferrard et al., 2017): 30-second clips in 15 top-level
  genres (the "Spoken" genre is excluded, it is speech, not music). About 2% of each
  genre (at least 8 clips) is held out for validation, every held-out clip is scored
  end to end at every evaluation, and everything else trains on random 20-second windows.
  In total the model saw about ten times the duration of the training audio.
- **Start**: random weights. The 45M checkpoints cannot warm-start a model of a
  different shape, so the loss begins near chance, ln 2048 = 7.62 (the first step
  measured 8.03), and falls steadily.
- **Learning rate was searched, briefly.** Six 600-step trials on a log grid from
  6e-5 to 6e-4 ended at validation loss 6.749, 6.747, 6.756 and 6.799 (the other two
  were pruned early). The peak learning rate **9.51e-5** won, narrowly: the three best
  rates were within 0.01 of each other, so the exact value matters little. Dropout was not searched.
- **Recipe**: AdamW (weight decay 0.1), 1,000-step warmup then cosine decay to
  9.5e-6, batch 32 × 20 s, gradient clipping at 1.0, bfloat16 autocast with
  float32 master weights and optimizer state.
- **Hardware**: 2× NVIDIA RTX A6000 with hand-written GPipe-style pipeline
  parallelism (the 16 blocks split across the two GPUs), gradient accumulation across
  micro-batches. 12,000 steps took 10.3 hours.
- **Validation loss** fell at every evaluation to **5.362** at step 12,000, which is the
  checkpoint released here. The gains had almost stopped (the last three evaluations
  improved by 0.005, 0.002 and 0.002, as the learning rate reached its floor).
- **Gradient norm** fell from about 1.3 at the start to a flat floor near 0.27 and stayed
  there; clipping at 1.0 only ever triggered during the first ~550 steps (the last logged value above 1.0 was at step 554).
- **Over-fitting has begun.** The gap between loss on held-out clips and on a
  same-size sample of training clips grew from 0.15 (step 4,000) to 0.25 (step 12,000).
  With about 0.15 billion audio tokens of data for a model of 1 billion parameters, more
  steps on this data would mostly memorise it.

## Limitations

- **Data-limited.** FMA medium is far too small for 1B parameters (a common rule of
  thumb asks for ~20 tokens per parameter; this run saw about 0.14 tokens per
  parameter of distinct data). That is why the model is only 0.035 nats better than
  the 45M one on the same clips.
- **Coarse prompts.** It saw 15 two-word captions, so it cannot follow free-form
  descriptions.
- **Noisy labels.** FMA genre tags are assigned by uploaders and are loose, so
  "pop" or "international" cover very different sounds.
- **Licence.** FMA tracks carry various Creative Commons licences, many of them
  non-commercial, so this model is for **research and educational use only**
  (CC-BY-NC-4.0).
- Mono, 32 kHz, at most 30 s per generation.

## Project

Built by [Khashayar Ghamati](https://ghamati.com). The write-up of this model —
scaling from 45M to 1B parameters, the training run, the KL-divergence comparison
and audio:
**[A Billion-Parameter Music Model: What 23× More Parameters Bought](https://ghamati.com/blog/music-llm-1b/)**

Related models: [music-llm-45m](https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m) (GTZAN) and
[music-llm-45m-fma](https://huggingface.co/khashayargh/music-llm-45m-fma) (FMA).

MiDashengLM-Spatial

Unifying General Audio Understanding and Spatial Awareness

[![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.11156-b31b1b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11156)  [![HuggingFace Model](https://img.shields.io/badge/HuggingFace-Model-FFD21E)](https://huggingface.co/mispeech/midashenglm-spatial)  [![Demo Page](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Page-0366d6)](https://jinbo-hu.github.io/midashenglm-spatial-demo/)  [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Repo-181717)](https://github.com/xiaomi-research/midashenglm-spatial) ## Overview **MiDashengLM-Spatial**, to our knowledge, is the **first open-source end-to-end** **unified** audio-language model that supports both **general audio understanding** and **spatial awareness** within a single architecture. It extends [MiDashengLM](https://github.com/xiaomi-research/dasheng-lm) with **Spatial-Dasheng** through a **hierarchical semantic-to-spatial conditioning (HSSC)** module to separately capture and effectively integrate semantic and spatial audio information. This design enables binaural perception and spatial audio understanding capabilities while preserving general audio understanding capabilities of the base model. ## Architecture ![Architecture](./assets/MiDashengLM-Spatial.png) ## Installation ```bash pip install torch torchaudio "transformers==4.57.6" einops ``` ## Usage ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "mispeech/midashenglm-spatial" # or a local package directory model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True) processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True) messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio", "path": "example/example.wav"}, # {"type": "audio", "audio": np.random.randn(2, 160000)}, {"type": "text", "text": "Write a general audio caption describing the sound source and its spatial information."}, ], }, ] with torch.no_grad(): inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, add_special_tokens=True, return_dict=True, ).to(model.device) generation = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=256, do_sample=False) print(processor.tokenizer.batch_decode(generation, skip_special_tokens=True)) ``` Put audio **before** text (the trained order), and feed real binaural `(2, T)` audio — mono still runs but carries no direction. ## Citation ```bibtex @article{hu2026midashenglmspatial, title={MiDashengLM-Spatial: Unifying General Audio Understanding and Spatial Awareness}, author={Jinbo Hu and Hang Su and Lichun Fan and Heinrich Dinkel and Gang Li and Zhanchen Dai and Yiru Zhang and Chang Liu and Peng Wang and Junnan Wu and Jian Luan and Cong Zou and Heng Qu}, year={2026}, journal={arXiv preprint arxiv:2610.11156}, } ``` ## License Released under the Apache License 2.0 (see [LICENSE](LICENSE)), for both research and commercial use.

# Ethio-Music-YuE2

Ethio-Music-YuE2 is a LoRA adapter for [YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) that steers it towards Ethiopian music:
- the six kiñit modes
- Ethiopian 6/8 and 4/4 grooves and Ethio-jazz
- Amharic lyrics

The repository also contains the code that turns tags and Amharic (Fidel) lyrics into a YuE2 request with a kiñit-constrained score.

**Use it with the kiñit score, which is the default.** With the score, the requested kiñit came out right in 72 of 72 test renders. From a caption alone, the adapter does much better than stock YuE2 but is still right only about half the time (see [Limitations](#limitations)).

| | |
|---|---|
| Base model | [m-a-p/YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) @ `8f24312`, decoder [m-a-p/YuE2-Vae](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-Vae) @ `152733a` |
| Adapter | LoRA, rank 64, on all 28 layers of YuE2's autoregressive (AR) branch. 69.7 M parameters, fp32, 279 MB. The NAR branch and the decoder are unchanged. |
| Training data | 756 songs (30.5 h) that YuE2-3B rendered from kiñit scores and that passed automatic quality gates, plus a regularizer of YuE2-generated songs. No real recordings. |
| Licence | CC BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial, inherited from YuE2-3B |

## Kiñits and grooves

| Kiñit | Scale degrees |
|---|---|
| tizita major | 1 2 3 5 6 |
| tizita minor | 1 2 ♭3 5 ♭6 |
| bati major | 1 3 ♯4 5 7 |
| bati minor | 1 ♭3 4 5 ♭7 |
| ambassel | 1 ♭2 4 5 ♭6 |
| anchihoye | 1 ♭2 4 ♭5 ♭7 |

Sources disagree on bati major (♮4 or ♯4) and anchihoye (6 or ♭7). This release uses ♯4 and ♭7.

Tizita major and bati minor are modes of one pentatonic collection, and the other four kiñits are modes of a second one. Within a collection, only the tonic tells the kiñits apart, so the scores anchor it.

**Grooves:**
- chikchika (6/8)
- eskista (6/8)
- slow 6/8
- shegaye (4/4)
- Ethio-jazz (12/8). The score writes it in 6/8, because YuE2 plays a 12/8 score as straight 4/4.

## How to use

You need the code in [`code/`](code/). Tested on Linux (WSL2) with an RTX 5090:

```bash
hf download Behailut/Ethio-Music-YuE2 --local-dir Ethio-Music-YuE2
cd Ethio-Music-YuE2/code
bash envs/setup_envs.sh ethioyue      # ~/envs/ethioyue: Python 3.12, torch 2.10 (CUDA 12.8), yue2-infer; needs uv

# the exact base-model commits the adapter was trained on
~/envs/ethioyue/bin/python scripts/fetch_models.py --only yue2 yue2_vae \
    --revision yue2=8f24312f187763b9854adeec87e437e2b03bbff1 \
    --revision yue2_vae=152733a19ad43aa67e367f9b5503ef8075bb5126

~/envs/ethioyue/bin/python scripts/30_generate.py \
    --lora ../ethio-music-yue2-ar-lora-r64.safetensors \
    --tags "<|tizita_minor, krar, 6/8 chikchika|>" \
    --lyrics my_song.txt --candidates 4 --out outputs/tizita_demo
```

`my_song.txt` contains Amharic lyrics in Fidel. Section lines are optional:

```
[Verse]
ትዝታ ትዝታ ልቤን ያስታውሰኛል
ፍቅርሽ ልቤን ወሰደው
```

**Input:**
- The lyrics are romanized automatically.
- Tags can name a kiñit, groove, genre, instrument, mood, vocal or production style (see `code/configs/taxonomy.yaml`).
- Leave out `--lyrics` for an instrumental.

**Output:** `best.flac` is the best of the candidates.

**Speed and memory:** a 40-second song took about 15 s per candidate and used about 8 GiB of VRAM.

**Settings:**
- Keep the defaults: `--composer kinit` (our score) and captions that name the scale degrees.
- `--composer none` (caption only) and `--composer planner` (YuE2 writes the score and we snap it into the kiñit) are weaker; see the results below.
- Don't use `--no-caption-degrees` with this adapter.

**Without our code:** the adapter keys are `layers.{i}.{self_attn|mlp}.{q,k,v,o,gate,up,down}_proj.lora_{A|B}`. They index YuE2's AR decoder layers (`model.model.layers[i]`).
- Merge with `W += lora_B @ lora_A` and scale 1.0, because alpha/rank is already folded into `lora_B`. See `code/ethioyue/train/lora.py` (`merge_lora`) and `adapter_config.json`.
- Name the scale degrees in your caption, e.g. `Ethiopian tizita minor pentatonic mode (scale degrees 1 2 b3 5 b6)`.
- Without our scores you get the caption-only or self-planned results below.

## Results

**Test set:**
- 18 prompts: 6 kiñits × 3 grooves (chikchika 6/8, Ethio-jazz, shegaye 4/4), all with the same Amharic lyrics.
- 2 seeds per prompt, and 4 seeds for the adapter on the score path.

**Metrics.** Every render was transcribed with [SheetSage2](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/SheetSage2).
- **Kiñit right:** the requested kiñit ranks first of the six at the requested tonic. Songs YuE2 plans itself pick their own tonic, so they are judged on the pitch collection instead.
- **Kiñit conformity:** the duration-weighted share of melody notes inside the kiñit.
- **Bar length held:** the transcribed bar is within 5% of the requested length, or of half or double it.
- **Tempo Acc2:** the tempo is within ±4%, allowing octave errors.
- **AudioBox PQ:** AudioBox-Aesthetics production quality, on a 1–10 scale.
- **Copy rate:** the share of generated 16-token windows that also appear in the training songs.

| How the song is requested | Metric | Stock YuE2-3B | With this adapter |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tags → our kiñit score** (recommended) | Kiñit right | 1.00 | **1.00** |
| | Kiñit conformity | 0.994 | 0.998 |
| | Bar length held | 1.00 | 0.96 |
| | Tempo Acc2 | 0.69 | 0.79 |
| | AudioBox PQ | 8.23 | 8.29 |
| **Caption; YuE2 writes its own score** | Right pitch collection | 0.33 | **0.61** |
| | Kiñit conformity | 0.83 | 0.90 |
| | Bar length held | 0.56 | **0.83** |
| | Ran to the length cap | 11% | **0%** |
| | AudioBox PQ | 8.29 | 8.24 |
| **Caption only** (no score) | Right pitch collection | 0.33 | **0.53** |
| | Kiñit conformity | 0.80 | 0.85 |
| | Bar length held | 0.28 | **0.56** |
| | AudioBox PQ | 8.29 | 8.26 |
| All | Copy rate vs training songs | – | 0 |

Each score-path cell covers 36 renders for stock YuE2 and 72 for the adapter. Every other cell covers 36.

**YuE2's own score snapped into the kiñit:** the kiñit was right in only 25 of 36 renders. Bati major and anchihoye fail most, so this mode isn't recommended.

**Right pitch collection by kiñit.** Six prompts each, with stock YuE2 given the same captions:

| Kiñit | Caption only: stock → adapter | YuE2 writes its score: stock → adapter |
|---|---|---|
| tizita major | 1.00 → 0.67 | 1.00 → 0.67 |
| tizita minor | 0.00 → 0.50 | 0.00 → 0.67 |
| bati major | 0.00 → 0.17 | 0.00 → 0.50 |
| bati minor | 1.00 → 1.00 | 0.83 → 0.83 |
| ambassel | 0.00 → 0.50 | 0.00 → 0.50 |
| anchihoye | 0.00 → 0.33 | 0.00 → 0.50 |

**Grooves from a caption alone** (bar length held, 12 prompts each):
- chikchika: 0.25 → 0.75
- shegaye: 0.50 → 0.83
- Ethio-jazz: 0.08 → 0.08

With the score, Ethio-jazz holds its bar in 24 of 24 renders.

## Limitations

- **Kiñit choice from a caption alone is not reliable.** Without a score, the right pitch collection comes out about half the time, with bati major at 17% and anchihoye at 33%. Use the kiñit score when the kiñit matters.
- **Tizita major got slightly worse.** The adapter traded some tizita major accuracy for the other kiñits: without a score it was right in 4 of 6 prompts instead of 6 of 6.
- **Ethio-jazz from a caption alone rarely holds its meter.** Use the score.
- **About 1 chikchika render in 8 loses its 6/8 grouping** and comes out grouped as 4/4 or 2/4, even with the score. Best-of-N selection checks the kiñit, not the meter, so listen and regenerate when this happens.
- **Amharic intelligibility has not been measured reliably.** Automatic speech recognition on sung vocals was too noisy to use: the character error rate was 0.64–0.86 on stock YuE2 and on an earlier adapter. No native-speaker listening test has been done yet.
- **No new timbres.** The training songs came from YuE2 itself, so the adapter re-weights what YuE2 can already do.
  - Krar, masenqo, washint, begena and kebero are requested through descriptive proxies such as "krar-like bright plucked bowl lyre", and they won't sound authentic.
  - Amharic ejectives are only approximated by the romanization.
- **The evaluation is automatic and small.** It relies on SheetSage2 transcription, beat tracking and AudioBox, over 18 prompts with 2–4 seeds. Treat small differences as noise.
- **Numbers in lyrics aren't converted.** Number-to-word normalization is off in this release, so write numbers and abbreviations as Amharic words.

## Training

**Data**
- **Prompts:** 1,000 prompts over 6 kiñits × 5 grooves. 60% are sung in Amharic and 40% are instrumental.
- **Scores:** each prompt got a kiñit score. 87% came from the bundled composer, and 13% were YuE2's own score snapped into the kiñit.
- **Rendering and gates:** YuE2-3B rendered every score, and SheetSage2 transcribed every render. A render was kept only if it met all of these:
  - kiñit conformity ≥ 0.90
  - bar length held
  - compound accents in 6/8 and 12/8 (salience ≥ 0.5)
  - length within 30% of the score
  - no truncation
- **Result:** 756 renders kept (76%, 30.5 h), split 719 for training and 37 for validation.
- **Captions** name the kiñit and its scale degrees, e.g. "Ethiopian tizita minor pentatonic mode (scale degrees 1 2 b3 5 b6), rolling 6/8 chikchika groove, 96 BPM".
- **Regularizer:** half of the training samples came from the regularizer pack of the [YuE2 minted corpus](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Mothersuperior/yue2-minted-corpus), 4,732 songs generated by YuE2-3B. It preserves YuE2's token grammar and general ability.
- **Lyrics:** lines from the [leyu-amharic](https://huggingface.co/leyu-amharic) transcripts (CC BY 4.0), plus 21 original lines, romanized with the bundled romanizer.

**Procedure** (full settings in `training_config.yaml`)
- **Adapter:** LoRA with rank 64, alpha 64 and no dropout, on the q/k/v/o and gate/up/down projections of all 28 AR layers.
  - The base model was frozen in bf16, and the adapter was trained in fp32.
  - The NAR branch and the decoder were not trained.
- **How songs were shown:** 50% caption only, 35% with the full score, 15% with the melody only. This way the adapter learns from text as well as from scores.
- **Balance:** sampling was split 50/50 between the two pitch collections. Otherwise the four-kiñit collection dominates.
- **Optimizer:** AdamW with learning rate 1e-4, betas 0.9/0.95 and no weight decay.
  - 50 warm-up steps, then a cosine schedule (3,000-step horizon, 20% floor), stopped at step 1,500.
  - Each step used 4 songs of up to 16,384 tokens, with gradient clipping at 1.0.
- **Compute:** 1 h 41 min on one RTX 5090, peaking at about 10 GiB.
- **Checkpoint choice:** the final checkpoint (step 1,500) was chosen over step 1,000 by caption-only generation results. Validation loss proved a misleading signal.

## Files

| File | Contents |
|---|---|

# OmniVoice LoRA — Ukrainian (uk)

Fine-tuned LoRA adapter for [OmniVoice](https://huggingface.co/k2-fsa/OmniVoice), adapted for Ukrainian speech synthesis and zero-shot voice cloning, with additional dictionary-guided stress training.

This LoRA is designed to help OmniVoice follow stress marks in Ukrainian text more accurately.

## Training Details

- **Base model:** k2-fsa/OmniVoice (Qwen3-0.6B backbone)
- **Method:** LoRA (rank=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05)
- **Target modules:** Language-model attention Q/K/V/O and MLP gate/up/down projections; audio embeddings and output heads also trained
- **Training data:** ~350 hours of Ukrainian speech samples with placed stress marks in text
- **Steps:** 20,150
- **Precision:** bf16
- **Hardware:** 4x RTX 6000 Pro Max-Q

## Usage

```python
import torch
import soundfile as sf
from omnivoice import OmniVoice
from peft import PeftModel

# Load the base model.
model = OmniVoice.from_pretrained(
    "k2-fsa/OmniVoice",
    device_map="cuda:0",
    dtype=torch.float16,
)

# Load the adapter on the full model, including its trained audio heads.
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(model, "dkaraush/omnivoice-lora-uk")
model = model.merge_and_unload().eval()

# Generate
with torch.inference_mode():
    audio = model.generate(
        text="Ба́ндами, послу́хай, новачки́, сте́жити, мальо́вана, раді́й, тридцяти́, поме́рти, яку́, це́гла, ім’я́, кві́тами, ду́мки, думки́, а́тлас, атла́с, бра́ти, брати́, пла́чу, плачу́, ко́си, коси́, ру́ки, руки́, повтори́.",
        language="uk",
    )[0]

sf.write("ukrainian.wav", audio, 24000)
```

The model card keeps this distinction explicit for reproducibility and attribution. ### Language and test accounting The canonical NOESIS claim for this bundle is **112 languages tested end-to-end (112/112)**. The 95-code family-adapter table below is a routing table for the documented family adapters, not the complete count of the NOESIS test surface. The legacy file named `manifest_94.json` is a partial adapter-sweep manifest and must not be interpreted as the total language coverage. # DuplexJev-4B-Para (v1.1)

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Research note: [keeping a speech-decision LLM able to talk](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-chat-replay.md)

**The small DuplexJev that hears the most beyond the words, and can still hold a normal conversation.**

> **v1.1 (2026-10-10)** replaces v1.0 (2026-10-09). v1.0 stays available as revision `v1.0`
> (`--revision v1.0` in vLLM, `revision="v1.0"` in `from_pretrained`).

Single-token decision training (one letter per answer) makes a speech LLM drift towards terse, one-line replies, and the
drift grows with every LoRA stacked on top. v1.1 mixes **conversation replay** into the same LoRA stage so the
model keeps the decision skills of v1.0 (spoken QA, gender, emotion, turn-taking, stress, non-verbal sounds, speaking
style, same-speaker) while answering free-form turns, multi-turn conversations included, like the original LLM.

Architecture: Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder + connector + Qwen3-4B, 4.2 B parameters, bf16,
~10 GB GPU memory.

**Which 4B to pick.** This one by default (it is the `duplexjev` package default). v1.0 if you only read single-token
decisions and need the last 1.5–2.6 points of emotion / VoiceBench or the higher sigh score; 4B-Turn if ZJU-ML and
turn-taking matter most; 4B-Stress if stress is the main thing you need.

## What changed

Starting from DuplexJev-4B-Turn: connector + a new rank-16 LoRA on the LLM (merged here), 4,000 steps. The mix is the v1.0 mix (4B-Turn mix, stress / pauses, speaker pairs, non-verbal sounds, speaking style, spoken multiple-choice replay; see revision `v1.0` for details) plus one more dataset (17.9 k items):

| added data | what it teaches |
|---|---|
| conversation replay: 13.4 k user turns (paralinguistic_dialogues with up to 6 earlier turns as text history, SmoothConv, AISHELL-1), target = the original Qwen3-4B's own reply to the transcript | keep normal, full-length replies and multi-turn behaviour |
| in-house chat items: 4.5 k, spoken (CosyVoice2) and typed | short everyday turns, repeat back what was said |

Two training details matter (both are in the open-source patches):

- replay rows get plain cross-entropy on the full reply. With the default mixed loss they would have gone to KL against
  a teacher that saw an empty message, and the model learned "you didn't send anything";
- **per-row** loss averaging. With token averaging, 256-token replies swamp the 1-token decision rows; stress scores fell
  12–20 points before this fix.

## Results

| | v1.0 | **v1.1** |
|---|---:|---:|
| qa100 / ZJU-ML | 79 / 50 | 77 / **58** |
| gender / emotion | 89.5 / 91.5 | 89.2 / 90.0 |
| VoiceBench OBQA / MMSU | 57.8 / 41.8 | 55.2 / 42.1 |
| Easy-Turn* | 91.5 | 91.0 |
| stress: DEBATE meaning / StressTest / StressPresso | 89.0 / 81.7 / 84.7 | 89.9 / 81.2 / 84.2 |
| laughter / breathing / cough / sigh (AUC, NonverbalTTS test) | 0.80 / 0.76 / 0.75 / 0.81 | 0.81 / 0.77 / 0.77 / **0.71** |
| laughter / breathing in natural Mandarin conversation (AUC) | 0.84 / 0.84 | 0.85 / **0.74** |
| speaking style, 7 classes (EARS) | 67% | 67% |
| multi-turn spoken conversation (mean reply tokens, cap 300) | 287 | 300 |

Paper protocol (single-token readout, PyTorch) for the decision rows. Through vLLM with `duplexjev-vllm` in the client
wording: qa100 76, ZJU-ML 51, gender 87.4, emotion 87.9, Easy-Turn 91.4 (v1.0: 76, 52, 87.2, 89.5, 91.2).

- \* Easy-Turn is in-domain.
- Single-turn spoken questions are still answered fairly briefly (about 40–50 tokens; the base LLM uses ~86). Multi-turn
  and typed chat are back to normal length.

## Serve with vLLM

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" duplexjev-vllm
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para --max-model-len 4096
# previous version: add --revision v1.0
```

Decision prompts are the same as for [DuplexJev-4B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Turn); see [`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py). Always offer a "none" option for stress and non-verbal questions. For
conversation, send the user audio as the user turn (`<|audio|>`) with ordinary chat history and sample as usual.

## Limitations

- Emotion is 1.5, VoiceBench OBQA 2.6 and spoken qa100 2 points below v1.0; sigh (NonverbalTTS) and
  breathing in natural conversation lose about 0.1 AUC.
- Asked about itself, it may describe abilities (seeing images, speaking) that this checkpoint does not have on its own:
  it takes speech and text and replies in text.
- Asked what it can do, it sometimes lists generic assistant skills (writing code, writing emails) beyond the training
  answers.
- Speaker judgments are coarse and must not be used to identify or verify people; emotion outputs must not be used to
  make decisions about individuals.

**CC BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial use only.**

- Non-commercial data:
  - Stress: DEBATE (github.com/SmileHnu/DEBATE), Stress-17K and TinyStress-15K (slprl);
  - Expresso (Meta), EARS (Meta) and NonVerbalSpeech-38K, all CC BY-NC 4.0;
  - ESD (research only); SmoothConv (CC BY-NC).
  - Conversation replay: user turns from wilzzzz/paralinguistic_dialogues (no licence stated on the dataset card; used for non-commercial research), SmoothConv (CC BY-NC), AISHELL-1 (Apache-2.0), LibriSpeech (CC BY 4.0); target replies generated by Qwen3-4B (Apache-2.0); spoken chat questions synthesised with CosyVoice2 (Apache-2.0).
- Other data:
  - VocalSound (CC BY-SA 4.0), NonverbalTTS (audio from VoxCeleb and Expresso);
  - VoxCeleb1 (CC BY 4.0), AISHELL-1 (Apache-2.0), LibriSpeech (CC BY 4.0);
  - ARC (CC BY-SA 4.0), OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA (MIT).
- Base models keep their licences: Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-ASR-0.6B are Apache-2.0 (Alibaba Cloud); the Qwen3-4B licence
  is included. The LLM weights are Qwen3-4B with LoRAs merged in.

# DuplexJev-32B-Para

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Research note: [teaching a speech-decision LLM to hear stress](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-stress-understanding.md)

**The DuplexJev model that hears the most beyond the words.** On top of everything
[DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn) and
[DuplexJev-32B-Stress](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Stress) do (spoken QA, gender, emotion,
turn-taking, stress and pauses), it also hears **laughter, breathing, coughs and sighs**, notices **how** someone is
talking (whispering, shouting, very fast or slow), and can tell, roughly as a person would, **whether two clips are
the same speaker**. Mandarin and English.

DuplexJev reads typed, closed-set decisions from speech as a **single-token distribution** of the LLM: zero decode
steps, many questions about the same clip in parallel. This repository is the complete model (Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder
+ connector + the language model of Qwen3-VL-32B, 33.0 B parameters, bf16; one 80 GB GPU).

**Which 32B to pick.** This one if you want the widest set of paralinguistic signals. Turn if every point of
emotion and turn-taking matters; Stress if stress is the main thing you need (see the table).

## What changed

Starting from DuplexJev-32B-Turn we trained the connector and a new rank-16 LoRA on the LLM (merged here) for 4,000
steps. The mix is the 32B-Turn mix plus:

| added data | what it teaches |
|---|---|
| stress / pause detection (as in 32B-Stress: DEBATE, Stress-17K, TinyStress-15K, Expresso, neutral negatives) | which word is stressed, or none; where the pause is |
| speaker pairs (VoxCeleb1 dev, AISHELL-1, LibriSpeech, two-speaker mixtures) | same speaker or not; is this person in the clip |
| non-verbal sounds (VocalSound, NonVerbalSpeech-38K, NonverbalTTS, Expresso laughing) | is there laughter / breathing / a cough / a sigh / sniffing / throat clearing / a sneeze / crying …; negatives are cut from the same recordings away from the event |
| speaking style (EARS, Expresso whisper) | whispering, loud, fast, slow, high or low pitch, normal |
| spoken multiple-choice replay (ARC, OpenBookQA and CommonsenseQA train splits read by TTS) | keeps "answer the content" from being crowded out by "listen to the voice" |

## Results

| | 32B-Turn | 32B-Stress | **32B-Para** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| qa100 / ZJU-ML | 96 / 87 | 96 / 87 | 95 / 87 |
| gender / emotion | 91.5 / 91.1 | 92.1 / 91.4 | 92.1 / 89.5 |
| VoiceBench OBQA‡ / MMSU | 85.5 / 72.1 | 86.2 / 71.4 | 90.1 / 73.4 |
| Easy-Turn* | 95.2 | 94.4 | 94.0 |
| which word is stressed, "none" offered: DEBATE (zh) / StressPresso (en) | 35 / 1 | 92 / 88 | 87 / 84 |
| neutral speech → "no word is stressed": AISHELL-1 / LibriSpeech | 92 / 50 | 99 / 99 | 99 / 100 |
| meaning from stress: DEBATE held-out / StressTest | 35 / 52 | 83 / 67 | 81 / 70 |
| **laughter / breathing / cough / sigh** (AUC, NonverbalTTS test, real speech, unseen) | — | 0.73 / 0.56 / 0.40 / 0.70 | **0.85 / 0.73 / 0.70 / 0.74** |
| **laughter / breathing in natural Mandarin conversation** (AUC, unseen third-party sample) | — | 0.61 / 0.44 | **0.80 / 0.78** |
| **speaking style, 7 classes** (EARS held-out speakers) | — | 45% | **69%** |
| **same speaker?** EER, AISHELL-1 same-gender pairs / VoxCeleb1-O | — | — | **18.2% / 38.5%** |

Paper protocol (single-token readout, PyTorch), % correct unless marked; AUC 0.5 = chance.
Through vLLM with `duplexjev-vllm` in the client wording: qa100 95, ZJU-ML 90, gender 91.9, emotion 89.5,
Easy-Turn 94.1 (DuplexJev-32B-Turn with the same harness: 97, 90, 92.4, 90.5, 95.6; qa100 and ZJU-ML have 100 items each).

- \* Easy-Turn is in-domain (its training split is in the mix).
- ‡ OpenBookQA's train split is in the replay data, so the OBQA gain is partly in-domain; MMSU is unrelated to it.
- For reference, an AudioSet AST tagger scores 0.71 / 0.75 / 0.85 / 0.76 on the same four sounds.
- Speaker: a dedicated speaker-verification model reaches ~1% EER on VoxCeleb1; this model is meant to have a rough,
  human-like sense of "same voice or not", not to identify people.

## Serve with vLLM

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" duplexjev-vllm
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Para --max-model-len 4096
```

Prompt format and client are the same as for [DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn);
see [`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py). Examples:

```
The user said: <|audio|>

Is there laughter in this audio?

Options:
A. Yes
B. No

Answer with the letter only.
```

```
用户说：<|audio|>

除了说话，这段音频里还有哪种声音？

A. 叹气
```

# Stable Audio 3 Optimized

> **Note:** This repository contains experimental checkpoints optimised for acceleration on specific hardware. For standard checkpoints, please use [Stable Audio 3 Medium](https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-audio-3-medium) instead.

Please note: For commercial use, please refer to [https://stability.ai/license](https://stability.ai/license)

## Model Description
`Stable Audio 3` is a family of fast latent diffusion models (small, medium, large) for variable length audio generation and editing. Since our models can generate several minutes of audio,
variable-length generations are key to avoid the cost of producing full-length generations for short
sounds. We also support inpainting, enabling targeted audio editing and the continuation of short
recordings. Our latent diffusion models operate on top of a novel semantic-acoustic autoencoder that
projects audio into a compact latent space, enabling efficient diffusion-based generation while preserving audio fidelity and encouraging semantic structure in the latent. Finally, we run adversarial
post-training to both accelerate inference and improve generation quality, reducing the number of inference steps while improving fidelity and prompt adherence. Stable Audio 3 models are trained on
licensed and Creative Commons data to generate music and sounds in less than a 2s on an H200 GPU
and less than a few seconds on a MacBook Pro M4. We release the weights of small and medium,
that can run on consumer-grade hardware, together with their training and inference pipeline.

## Usage

This model can be used with:
1. the [`stable-audio-3`](https://github.com/Stability-AI/stable-audio-3) inference and fine-tuning library
2. the [`stable-audio-tools`](https://github.com/Stability-AI/stable-audio-tools) research library


### Using with `stable-audio-3`
```python
from stable_audio_3 import StableAudioModel

model = StableAudioModel.from_pretrained("medium")
audio = model.generate(
    prompt=(
        "House music that encapsulates the feeling of being at a festival "
        "in the sunny weather with all your friends 124 BPM"
    ),
    duration=180
)
```

### Using with `stable-audio-tools`
```python
import torch
import torchaudio
from einops import rearrange
from stable_audio_tools import get_pretrained_model
from stable_audio_tools.inference.generation import generate_diffusion_cond_inpaint

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
if device == "cuda":
  model_half = True

# Download model
model, model_config = get_pretrained_model("stabilityai/stable-audio-3-medium")
sample_rate = model_config["sample_rate"]
sample_size = model_config["sample_size"]

model = model.to(device)
if model_half:
  model = model.to(torch.float16)
# Set up text and timing conditioning
conditioning = [{
    "prompt": (
        "A dream-like Synthpop instrumental that would accompany "
        "a dream-sequence in a surrealist movie 120 BPM"
    ),
    "seconds_total": 380
}]

# Generate stereo audio
output = generate_diffusion_cond_inpaint(
    model,
    steps=8,
    cfg_scale=1.0,
    conditioning=conditioning,
    sample_size=sample_size,
    sampler_type="pingpong",
    device=device
)

# Rearrange audio batch to a single sequence
output = rearrange(output, "b d n -> d (b n)")

# Peak normalize, clip, convert to int16, and save to file
output = output.to(torch.float32).div(torch.max(torch.abs(output))).clamp(-1, 1).mul(32767).to(torch.int16).cpu()
torchaudio.save("output.wav", output, sample_rate)
```


### Optimized CPU runtime (TFLite / LiteRT)

Portable CPU builds live in [`optimized/tflite`](https://github.com/Stability-AI/stable-audio-3/tree/main/optimized/tflite). The SAME autoencoder ships as static **rung** `.tflite` codecs at `tflite/same-{s,l}/{enc,dec}_{fp32,w8a8}.tflite` — one weight-shared file per encoder/decoder that dispatches a fixed-size subgraph per length, keeping RAM flat and avoiding a chunk-size knob. They require **`ai_edge_litert>=2.2.0`** and are driven by the `RungEncoder` / `RungDecoder` runtime in that directory (`w8a8` is the default; `fp32` is the bit-exact reference). The earlier dynamic-length codecs are preserved under `tflite/same-*/legacy/`.

### Runtime LoRA on TensorRT (NVIDIA)

`dit_fp16_lora.trt` is a DiT with a **runtime low-rank branch** on each adapted linear. All
three DiTs have one:

| engine | DiT | targets | size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tensorRT/sm_90/sa3-m/dit_fp16_lora.trt` | medium, 24 × 1536 | 229 | 2.96 GB |
| `tensorRT/sm_90/sa3-sm-music/dit_fp16_lora.trt` | small-music, 20 × 1024 | 193 | 0.95 GB |
| `tensorRT/sm_90/sa3-sm-sfx/dit_fp16_lora.trt` | small-sfx, 20 × 1024 | 193 | 0.95 GB |

A TensorRT plan has its weights compiled in, so an adapter cannot be merged into it the way
the CPU runtime does; these engines instead take the adapter as *network inputs* — `A`, `Bt`
and a per-output-row rescale `P` are fed in like activations, with the rank as a dynamic
dimension — and compute `y = W₀·x·(1+P) + Btᵀ·(srow ⊙ (A·x))`.

So loading an adapter is a buffer write rather than a rebuild: adapters swap in milliseconds,
several stack by concatenating along the rank axis (up to a total of 512), and `srow` gives
each one its own strength. `P` is what DoRA needs — its per-row magnitude rescale is a change
to the *base* path that no low-rank branch can express.

The branch costs a flat few ms per step, so its relative price depends on which DiT it is
attached to. On medium that is +13% at L=4096 and +37% at 1292; on the small DiTs the same
absolute cost lands on a base step about 2.7× cheaper, so at stack rank 16 on an H200 it is
+34% at L=4096, +60% at 1292 and +83% at 323. It is paid even with an *empty* stack — in fact
rank 1 is the most expensive configuration, since TensorRT picks a worse tactic below rank 8
— so use `dit_fp16.trt` until an adapter is actually wanted. That matters more on the small
DiTs than on medium.

**Adapters are not portable between the three DiTs**: different depth and width, so a medium
adapter will not load against a small engine.

**sm_90 only**; other architectures build locally in ~5–8 min, since TensorRT bakes the GPU
architecture into the plan. The runtime, the adapter row-norm baking step and the layer maps
all live in
[`optimized/tensorRT/scripts/lora`](https://github.com/Stability-AI/stable-audio-3/tree/main/optimized/tensorRT/scripts/lora)
— this repository holds only the compiled plans.

## Model Details
* **Model type**: `Stable Audio 3` is a latent diffusion model based on a transformer architecture.
* **Language(s)**: English
* **License**: [Stability AI Community License](https://stability.ai/license).
* **Research Paper**: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17991](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17991)

We use a publicly available pre-trained T5Gemma model ([t5gemma-b-b-ul2](https://huggingface.co/google/t5gemma-b-b-ul2)) for text conditioning. T5Gemma is redistributed under the [Gemma Terms of Use](LICENSE_GEMMA.md).

## Training dataset

### Datasets Used
Our dataset consists of 1,278,902 audio recordings, where 806,284 recordings are licensed from [AudioSparx](https://www.audiosparx.com/) and a further 472,618 are from [Freesound](https://freesound.org/). 
The Freesound portion consists of recordings licensed under CC-0, CC-BY, or CCSampling+. To ensure no copyrighted content was present in the Freesound data, music recordings were identified
using the PANNs [89] tagger. We flagged audio that activated music-related tags for at least 30s (threshold of 0.15),
that was sent to a trusted content detection company to verify the absence of copyrighted material. All identified copyrighted content was removed. After filtering, the Freesound part includes 266,324 CC-0, 194,840 CC-BY, and 11,454
CC-Sampling+ recordings. The same subset of Freesound audio we used to train Stable Audio Open: https://info.stability.ai/attributions.

# OmniVoice — single-file ComfyUI checkpoints

Single-file checkpoints of [k2-fsa/OmniVoice](https://huggingface.co/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) (Qwen3 LLM + HiggsAudioV2 codec), repacked for [ComfyUI-OmniVoice-Native](https://github.com/Aero-Ex/ComfyUI-OmniVoice). Config, codec config, and BPE tokenizer are embedded as safetensors metadata — no sidecar files needed.

## Files

- `omnivoice.safetensors` (3.3GB, full quality) — most robust, recommended for tags + voice-design prompts.
- `omnivoice-int8.safetensors` (1.1GB, INT8-ConvRot) — same quality on plain prompts, smaller download. ~86% top-1 agreement with full.

## Use

1. Install the pack: ComfyUI Manager → search `OmniVoice`, or `git clone https://github.com/Aero-Ex/ComfyUI-OmniVoice` into `ComfyUI/custom_nodes/`. No `pip install` needed.
2. Put a file from this repo into `ComfyUI/models/omnivoice/`.
3. `Load OmniVoice Model` → `OmniVoice Generate`. For a designed voice, add `OmniVoice Voice Design` → `instruct`.

Defaults: 32 steps, guidance 2.0, 25 tok/s. `num_steps` 16 roughly halves generation time. Texts over ~30s are auto-split into ~15s chunks and cross-faded.

## Notes

- Voice clone: `ref_audio` + `ref_text` (transcript required, no ASR). One voice per Generate call — multi-speaker dialogue = one Generate per speaker, then concat.
- Voice design: gender, age, pitch, whisper, English accent / Chinese dialect via the `instruct` string.
- Vocalization tags (exact spelling, spoken by the model): `[laughter]`, `[sigh]`, `[question-en]`, `[question-ah]`, `[question-oh]`, `[question-ei]`, `[question-yi]`, `[confirmation-en]`, `[surprise-ah]`, `[surprise-oh]`, `[surprise-wa]`, `[surprise-yo]`, `[dissatisfaction-hnn]`.

  ```
  Wait, what [surprise-ah]? You finished it already [question-oh]? Ha [laughter]! I knew you could do it [confirmation-en]. Phew [sigh], now we can finally rest.
  ```

- Keep normal punctuation spacing around tags (`! Ha`, `. Phew`, never `!Ha`). Crushed punctuation derails takes, especially on INT8.
- Same seed can give different takes across checkpoints — test seeds 1–3 per setup and pin the keeper.
- No output post-processing — use standard ComfyUI audio nodes for gain/fades/trim.

# VocoLoco — OmniVoice for the browser

[k2-fsa/OmniVoice](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) converted for text-to-speech that runs entirely in the browser with [VocoLoco](https://github.com/Magkino/vocoloco_tts): weights for VocoLoco's own WebGPU engine (`engine/`), and ONNX exports for ONNX Runtime Web, the fallback for browsers without the engine's WebGPU features.

## Files

### WebGPU engine (`engine/`)

Each model is a JSON manifest (tensor names, shapes, offsets) and one binary file with the weights.

| File | Size | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| `engine/omnivoice-f16.json` + `.bin` | 1.1 GB | Main TTS model, f16 weights |
| `engine/decoder-f32.json` + `.bin` | 85 MB | Audio decoder (tokens to 24 kHz waveform), f32 |
| `engine/encoder-f32.json` + `.bin` | 622 MB | Audio encoder for voice cloning, f32 |

### ONNX (ONNX Runtime Web)

| File | Size | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| `omnivoice-main-split.onnx` + `omnivoice-main.onnx_data_00`–`_04` | 2.3 GB | Main TTS model (FP32, sharded; shards listed in `omnivoice-main-manifest.json`) |
| `omnivoice-decoder.onnx` | 83 MB | Audio decoder (tokens to waveform) |
| `omnivoice-encoder-fixed.onnx` | 624 MB | Audio encoder for voice cloning |

### Shared

| File | Size | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| `omnivoice-config.json` | <1 KB | Model config |
| `tokenizer.json`, `tokenizer_config.json` | 11 MB | Qwen2 BPE text tokenizer |

## Usage

These files are made for [VocoLoco](https://github.com/Magkino/vocoloco_tts), a fully client-side TTS application ([live](https://magkino.github.io/vocoloco_tts/)). No server required.

## Architecture

# diffrhythm-1.2-p100a

DiffRhythm 1.2 Full, ported to one Tenstorrent Blackhole p100a.
Weights: [ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm-1_2-full](https://huggingface.co/ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm-1_2-full) · Upstream code: [ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm](https://github.com/ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm) · Port: [SunandBean/tt-diffrhythm](https://github.com/SunandBean/tt-diffrhythm)

Runs on **p100a** (mesh 1×1). The **CFM transformer and the stable-audio VAE decoder run on the card**; the style encoder, the sampler and the post-processing stay on the CPU.

**What this port adds** — the CFM transformer and the stable-audio-tools Oobleck decoder on the card, sharing the worker, transport and host helpers with the sibling [tt-acestep](https://github.com/SunandBean/tt-acestep) port.
**What it builds on** — DiffRhythm's own pipeline (Apache-2.0), which runs unchanged on the CPU; only those two stages move.

**A 96-second song in 10.0 s** end to end — the CFM transformer 7.7 s across 62 calls, the audio VAE decode 2.0 s. The same song takes 9.7–10.1 s on an RTX 5070 Ti.

## Listen

Exactly what the container returned on run 1 of the measurement below — `POST /predict` with
`{"prompt": "warm lo-fi hip hop, mellow rhodes piano, soft vinyl crackle, relaxed drums",
"instrumental": true, "duration": 96, "seed": 42}`, generated in **10.05 s** on the card. The file is
the response's WAV bytes, unmodified: 96.0 s stereo 44.1 kHz 16-bit, sha256 `7e89a573e6d94e4f`.

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/sunandbean/diffrhythm-1.2-p100a/resolve/main/media/diffrhythm_96s_instrumental.wav"></audio>

[`media/diffrhythm_96s_instrumental.wav`](media/diffrhythm_96s_instrumental.wav) (16 MB)

## How it is wired

Two stages move to the card and nothing else changes: `remote.py` replaces `cfm.transformer` with a `RemoteDiffRhythmDiT` and decodes through a `RemoteVae`, so the upstream `CFM.sample` loop runs unmodified.

Both shims reach the card through exactly one method, `worker.call(msg)`, and there are two things that answer it.

**Two processes** (`TTWorker`), when DiffRhythm and tt-metal cannot share an interpreter — which is the deployment this port came from, where DiffRhythm resolved `torch 2.10.0+cu128` and `numpy>=2` against ttnn's `torch 2.11.0+cpu` and `numpy 1.x`:

```
  DiffRhythm venv (CPU)                    TT image (p100a)
  ─────────────────────                    ────────────────
  style encoder                ──socket──► worker.py
  CFM sampler loop                         DiffRhythmDiT  (on the card)
  post-processing                          OobleckTT      (on the card)
```

Tensors cross as raw little-endian bytes with a dtype and a shape (`wire.py`), because the two sides cannot share a pickle of a torch tensor.

**One process** (`LocalWorker`), when one environment satisfies both — which is what the container below is. `LocalWorker` answers the same `call(msg)` in-process, so the shims, their window arithmetic and their drop-in signatures are reused unchanged rather than reimplemented.

Messages still carry `wire`-encoded tensors in that case even though both ends are one process. That is deliberate: it is what lets the shims run against either worker, and the encoding is a float32 copy of a few MB against card work measured in seconds.

## Quickstart

Prerequisite: a tt-metal / ttnn environment for the worker, and DiffRhythm installed in its own environment for the host side.

```bash
hf download sunandbean/diffrhythm-1.2-p100a --include "code/*" --local-dir diffrhythm-1.2-p100a && cd diffrhythm-1.2-p100a
pip install -e code/
```

Host side, inside the DiffRhythm environment:

```python
from tt_diffrhythm import TTWorker, RemoteDiffRhythmDiT, RemoteVae

worker = TTWorker(cfm_model_pt, model="diffrhythm", vae=vae_model_pt).start()
worker.wait_ready()
cfm.transformer = RemoteDiffRhythmDiT(worker, cfm.transformer)
...                                          # upstream CFM.sample runs unchanged
audio = RemoteVae(worker, upsample=2048)(latents)
worker.close()
```

Worker side, inside the tt-metal image:

```bash
python -m tt_diffrhythm.worker --socket /ipc/worker.sock \
  --checkpoint /checkpoint/cfm_model.pt --vae /vae/vae_model.pt
python -m tt_diffrhythm.warm_cache     # compile every sequence bucket ahead of time
```

| | |
|---|---|
| **Duration** | 96–285 seconds |
| **Lyrics** | Plain lyrics with estimated line timing, or a timestamped LRC |
| **Guidance** | CFG: `pred + 4 (pred − null)` — every step runs two DiT calls |
| **Shapes** | Song lengths fall into sequence buckets (`diffrhythm_host.seq_buckets`), both CFG branches, plus the VAE windows. `warm_cache` compiles all of them. |

## Performance

Measured on an idle p100a. A 96-second song is 2067 latent frames, padded to a sequence of 2560.

| | |
|---|---:|
| **DiT, whole 96-second song** | **8.9 s** (7.7 s at HiFi2) |
| One DiT call at sequence 2560 | 121 ms |
| Per call during the device check | 0.143–0.186 s |

Where a 121 ms call goes (`dit_profile.py`, 156.8 ms profiled):

| Op | Time | Calls |
|---|---:|---:|
| matmul | 66.6 ms | 66 |
| SDPA | 21.9 ms | 16 |
| add | 12.0 ms | 47 |
| RMS norm | 7.7 ms | 32 |
| slice | 7.3 ms | 62 |
| rotary embedding | 5.2 ms | 32 |

The audio VAE decoder, against a CPU decode of the same latents:

| Latent frames | CPU | p100a (first / warm) |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 512 | 10.67 s | 33.94 / **0.33** s |
| 1024 | — | 0.81 s |

The first decode at a shape pays the kernel compilation; afterwards it is 30× faster than the CPU.

### From the published container

The same image anyone can `tt-model pull`, reached over its own HTTP server on an idle card
(2026-10-09). Three 96-second instrumentals, seed 42, from a cold start:

| | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Generation** | **10.05 s** | 10.06 s | 10.04 s |
| CFM transformer, 62 calls | 7.68 s | 7.68 s | 7.69 s |
| VAE decode | 2.03 s | 2.05 s | 2.01 s |

All three returned the same 96.0 s stereo 44.1 kHz WAV. Load to ready was 50 s, of which the VAE
warm-up is 3.1 s; device DRAM after load is 2.9 GB of 29.9 — the card is nowhere near full, and
the port holds that headroom deliberately so the sequence buckets can grow to 285 seconds.

The whole request takes about 30 s of wall time, because the response carries the song: 17 MB of
WAV, base64-encoded. Generation is the 10 s above; the rest is serialising and shipping it.

### Against an RTX 5070 Ti

DiffRhythm's own GPU path with the deployment's stage-by-stage placement (one model in VRAM at a
time, which is what keeps it inside 16 GB), same prompt and duration, a fresh seed per run:

| | p100a (container) | RTX 5070 Ti |
|---|---:|---:|
| 96-second instrumental | 10.04–10.06 s | **9.73–10.05 s** |
| First run | 10.05 s | 12.35 s |
| Peak device memory | 2.9 GB of 29.9 | 2.5 GB of 15.5 |

The same, within noise. The card reaches it with the CFM transformer and the audio VAE decoder in
TTNN and everything else on the CPU; the GPU reaches it by moving three models in and out of VRAM.

### Accuracy

**The torch reference in this port against upstream DiffRhythm** (float32, per CFM call): PCC **0.9999997–0.9999999**. For scale, upstream float32 against the GPU fp16 run is 0.999995–0.999999 — so the reimplementation is closer to upstream than upstream is to its own GPU run.

**The card against this port's reference**: minimum PCC **0.99994** across the whole 96-second song.

**Final latents against the GPU fp16 run**, which is what actually matters after CFG amplification:

| | Final latent PCC | Relative RMS |
|---|---:|---:|
| CPU float32 | 0.99997 | 0.008 |
| **p100a (HiFi4, the default)** | **0.9954** | 0.096 |
| p100a (HiFi2) | 0.9931 | 0.118 |
| CPU bf16 | 0.99129 | 0.132 |

**The card beats a CPU bf16 run.** Decoded audio against the GPU: PCC 0.9721 and 2.06 dB spectral distance, against 0.9691 and 3.07 dB for CPU bf16 (CPU float32 is 0.9996 / 0.51 dB). The audio VAE decoder itself is PCC 0.99963 with 0.93 dB spectral distance against the CPU.

CFG is why the margin matters: `pred + 4 (pred − null)` multiplies the difference between the two branches by four, so a small per-call error is amplified before it reaches the audio. `DRPrecision` therefore keeps the activations, the residual and the output in fp32 and defaults to HiFi4 matmuls — HiFi2 is about 14% faster and measurably worse.

## Caveats

- **Single card only.** Mesh 1×1.
- **Seeds do not reproduce across backends.** A song made on the p100a cannot be reproduced bit-for-bit on a GPU with the same seed.
- **Two environments, or one.** Where DiffRhythm's environment and the tt-metal runtime cannot be merged, the host side runs inside DiffRhythm's own environment and the worker inside a tt-metal image. Where they can — which the container below is — `LocalWorker` runs both in one process. Which one you get is a property of the environment, not of the port.
- **CFG doubles the work.** Every sampler step is two DiT calls, one conditional and one null.
- The first song of each shape pays the kernel compilation, and so does the first VAE decode at a shape (33.9 s against 0.33 s warm). Run `warm_cache` after changing the code or the image.
- A render holds the card for the length of the song. On a shared card that blocks everything else.

## Licensing

- Weights: [ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm-1_2-full](https://huggingface.co/ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm-1_2-full), Apache-2.0. Not redistributed here.
- Port code (`code/tt_diffrhythm/`): Apache-2.0, from [SunandBean/tt-diffrhythm](https://github.com/SunandBean/tt-diffrhythm).
- `code/{model,infer,g2p,config,dataset}/` are **DiffRhythm itself** (Apache-2.0), at [`28ad63c`](https://github.com/ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm/commit/28ad63c0f096fe2ee258bcabbcf081d5d9366afd), unmodified. They ship here because the container runs them: upstream is a research checkout with no packaging, so it is vendored as source rather than resolved by pip. `code/models/` is [tt-metal](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal)'s `models/common` and `models/tt_dit` (Apache-2.0), for the same reason.
- `code/tt_diffrhythm/common.py` and the worker, transport and audio VAE modules are shared with the sibling [tt-acestep](https://github.com/SunandBean/tt-acestep) port (Apache-2.0); `oobleck_vae.py` implements both DiffRhythm's stable-audio-tools decoder and ACE-Step's diffusers Oobleck decoder.

## Run it as a container

Everything below is generated by `tt-model package` from the manifest this image was built from.

```bash
tt-model pull  sunandbean/diffrhythm-1.2-p100a --with-weights
tt-model serve sunandbean/diffrhythm-1.2-p100a
```

`pull --with-weights` downloads the Docker image and the [`ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm-1_2-full`](https://huggingface.co/ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm-1_2-full) weights (into your HF cache; they are not in the image). `serve` starts the model's own HTTP server on port 20000 (or the next free port, if that one is busy); the first start compiles kernels for your device, which takes several minutes, and the server is ready when it logs `Application startup complete`.

### Request shape

`POST /predict` takes `{"prompt": str, "lyrics": str, "instrumental": bool,
"duration": int, "seed": int}` and returns a base64 WAV with `timing_s` and the `lrc` the
song was actually sung to.

`prompt` is the style description. Vocals need `lyrics`: real LRC is used as given, and
plain lines get approximate starts derived from their word counts -- a convenience, not
learned alignment. `duration` is 96-285 seconds; use the ACE-Step port for longer songs.
The schedule is fixed at **32 steps**; any other `inference_steps` is a 422.
